analysis.one_liner: Shields gun makers and sellers from most lawsuits over criminal misuse of their firearms.
analysis.headline: The Senate put the bill on its calendar the week it was introduced and never voted on it; a nearly identical liability shield for the gun industry became law in 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would bar any lawsuit in state or federal court against firearm and ammunition manufacturers, dealers, and sellers for harm caused when someone criminally or unlawfully misuses a gun, and would immediately dismiss lawsuits already pending when it became law. It leaves narrow exceptions, including cases of negligent entrustment, knowing statutory violations tied to the harm, and injuries from actual product defects. The bill was introduced in the Senate in late October 2003, placed on the Senate calendar within days, and never received a vote before that Congress ended. A companion measure with the same name passed and was signed into law in 2005.
analysis.who_benefits: Firearms and ammunition manufacturers, importers, distributors, dealers, and their trade associations gain, because the main legal tool being used against them — civil suits seeking damages for gun violence — would be shut off in both state and federal courts, including suits already filed by cities and states.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Firearm and ammunition makers and sellers

how_it_helps.text: Bars any 'qualified civil liability action' — a suit against a manufacturer or seller of a firearm, ammunition, or components for damages from criminal or unlawful misuse by anyone — from being brought in any state or federal court [S2] [S3].
Requires courts to immediately dismiss any such lawsuit pending on the date of enactment, wiping out suits already filed [S2] [S3].
Extends the shield to trade associations of manufacturers and sellers, and declares that Congress will protect the industry's ability to speak, assemble, and petition the government [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Shooting victims and their families, and the cities and states that had filed suits seeking to recover gun-violence costs, would lose their day in court against gun sellers whose distribution practices allegedly supplied criminals, with only the narrow exceptions listed in the bill left open.
analysis.who_pays_short: Shooting victims, families, and suing cities

drawbacks.text: It would end, retroactively, lawsuits already in progress by governments and private plaintiffs, eliminating their only remedy short of new legislation [S3].

The bill's carve-outs are narrow: negligent entrustment, knowing and willful statutory violations that proximately caused the harm, knowing transfers to convicted violent or drug-trafficking felons, contract and warranty claims, and true design or manufacturing defects [S2] [S3]. Theories used in the pending suits — that oversaturated, negligent distribution created the harm — would largely fall outside them.

The industry's own stated rationale is that lawsuits against makers of products that function as designed are an 'abuse of the legal system' that burdens interstate commerce [S3]. The honest counterweight is that litigation was, at the time, the main mechanism pressing sellers on how their guns reached criminals, and the bill removes it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Supporters had a real point: manufacturers of products that work as intended are normally not liable for a third party's crime, and a wave of suits designed to bleed an industry through court costs is a legitimate concern. But the bill does not merely restore the common-law baseline — it wipes out pending suits, including those by cities that had already invested years in them, and blocks state courts from applying their own tort law to gun distribution. The cost falls on victims of gun violence and their communities, while the benefit is concentrated in one industry.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate put it on its calendar within days of introduction and never brought it to a vote before that Congress ended; a nearly identical bill became law in the next Congress.

narrative.text: Sen. Larry Craig introduced the bill on October 31, 2003, and it was read and placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar the same day [S1] [S5].
On November 3, 2003, it was read a second time and placed on the calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 364 — the queue of bills awaiting floor action [S5] [S3].
No further action was ever taken: the action history shows no committee markup, no debate, and no vote before the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005 [S5] [S1].

The bill's findings acknowledge that liability suits had already been commenced or contemplated by the federal government, states, municipalities, and private groups — the actions this bill would bar and dismiss [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: On this bill alone, shooting victims and the cities suing gun sellers kept their claims alive, since nothing passed. But the industry did not have to wait long: Congress passed and the President signed an essentially identical Protection of Lawful Commerce in Arms Act in 2005, so firearm manufacturers and sellers ultimately received the shield this bill sought.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Gun makers, via the identical 2005 law

for.name: Sen. Larry Craig
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and got it placed on the Senate calendar within days; no cosponsors were listed

for.name: National Rifle Association
for.what_they_did: Championed the Protection of Lawful Commerce in Arms Act; the bill's findings and purposes track its position, and the measure shielded trade associations like itself from suits

sides.party_line_note: No debate or votes were ever recorded and the bill carried zero cosponsors, so its partisan shape cannot be read from this Congress's record; its 2005 counterpart, however, passed both chambers with broad bipartisan majorities.

industries.industry: Firearms and ammunition manufacturers, importers, dealers, and sellers
industries.note: The bill would make the industry effectively immune to civil suits for harms caused by criminal misuse of its products, dismissing suits already pending. The public's interest in holding sellers accountable for how guns reach criminals runs directly against the industry's interest here.

Trade associations are themselves named as protected defendants, and the bill's stated purposes include protecting their advocacy activities. Their gain in legal protection comes at the cost of victims' and cities' claims.

industries.industry: Municipal and state governments pursuing gun-liability litigation
industries.note: The bill's own findings acknowledge suits commenced or contemplated by federal, state, and municipal governments, and it would dismiss pending ones. Those governments were acting to recover community gun-violence costs on behalf of residents.
